performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How does a fast piece sound like many voices at once?
intro: Women quarrel and gossip in a French market. The piece is a rapid scherzo: chattering music in E♭, a contrasting middle that builds to one huge climax, the chatter again, and a short slower coda that runs on into the Catacombs. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: Contrasting middle · building to the climax
The chatter returns
sections.mNote: opening material returns after the climax and a hush

cues.title: A busy violin idea
cues.text: A busy violin idea sets the gossip going, taken up by woodwinds and percussion including celesta. Horns add emphasis, but Ravel keeps the large ensemble light by passing the scurrying idea between sections.
cues.evidence: Violin idea, woodwinds, celesta, horns and the passing of the idea between sections: Philharmonia guide (Joanna Wyld). Onsets per second 4.4, 3.8, 2.6 at 0:00–0:10; relative level −18.4 to −16.1 dB. The report does not identify instruments.

cues.title: A cow, false teeth and a red nose
cues.text: Mussorgsky’s manuscript carried a French note, later crossed out, of the great news: a recovered cow, a lady’s new porcelain teeth, a gentleman’s nose as red as a peony. Stasov called the picture French women quarrelling in the market.
cues.evidence: Crossed-out programme and its details: Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note (https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky) and Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition); Stasov’s description: Wikipedia, movement 7. The note sits where the level is moderate (−17 to −13 dB, 0:20–0:30).

cues.title: Surges towards the peak
cues.text: From about 0:43 the level surges in stages, from about −22 dB at 0:40 to −8 dB at 0:47 and again at 0:54, towards the loudest passage of the movement. The chatter does not slow as it grows.
cues.evidence: Strongest boundary at 0:46 (novelty 1.00). A 1-second pass gives −21.8 dB (0:40), −8.1 dB (0:47), −8.2 dB (0:54) and −2.4 dB (0:58) at three to six detected attacks a second. The report’s 5-second table shows −18.3 dB (0:40) and −6.5 dB (0:55).

cues.title: The loudest moment, then a hush
cues.text: At about 0:58 the sound peaks at its loudest, then falls by roughly twenty decibels within three seconds. In Lamm’s score the opening E♭ music returns at bar 27 of about 40, close to this hush by proportion; here the chatter climbs back from about 1:02.
cues.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −2.4 dB at 0:58, −4.7 dB at 0:59, −18.8 dB at 1:00 and −23.0 dB at 1:01, a fall of 20.6 dB in three seconds; the report shows the two quietest windows at 1:00 and 1:05 and a boundary at 1:02 (novelty 0.97). The return of the E♭ material at bar 27 of about 40 is in Lamm’s score (Mutopia, limoges.ly); its placement near 1:00–1:05 is by proportion, not an alignment.

cues.title: The climb back
cues.text: After the hush the level climbs again, from about −14 dB at 1:10 to −7 dB near 1:24, as the opening chatter builds once more. At about 1:26 the music stops for a moment before the final bars.
cues.evidence: Relative level −13.8 dB (1:10), −12.6 (1:15), −9.9 (1:20); a 1-second pass gives −7.3 dB at 1:24 and −30.3 dB at 1:26; boundaries at 1:18 and 1:24 (novelty 0.46, 0.52). The chatter’s return after the climax is the written order in Lamm’s score (bar 27).

cues.title: Slower, straight into the Catacombs
cues.text: A pause of about a second near 1:26 is probably the fermata the score places before the last four bars, marked “Meno mosso, sempre capriccioso”. The level peaks at −4.2 dB near 1:38, and the Catacombs follows without a break.
cues.evidence: A frame-by-frame level pass finds near-silence between 1:26.1 and 1:27.3, then −8.8 dB (1:28), −5.5 (1:32) and −4.2 dB (1:38) with brightness 3,011 Hz and no detected attacks at 1:39. The fermata in bar 36, the Meno mosso mark in bars 37–40 and the attacca are in Lamm’s score (Mutopia, limoges.ly); the match to the pause is by proportion.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The chatter gives way to a new key
transitions.how: At about bar 12 the E♭ chatter gives way to a contrasting middle written with the key signature of C major, then in 3/4 from bar 16 and 4/4 from bar 24. In this recording the strongest early boundary falls at 0:30, with a spike in level at 0:28. The change is of key and metre, not of speed: the scherzo’s quick pace carries on.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:30 (novelty 0.94); a 1-second pass shows −6.2 dB at 0:28 against −12 to −17 dB at 0:26–0:30. Key signatures and metres: Lamm’s score (Mutopia, limoges.ly), bars 12, 16 and 24, placed by proportion (bar 12 of about 40 is near 0:30). The score is read by key signature; the report’s key estimates are not used.

transitions.title: A peak, a hush, then E♭ again
transitions.how: The middle builds in stages to its loudest chords near 0:58 and the level collapses by some twenty decibels within three seconds. In the score the opening E♭ music returns at bar 27, which falls near this hush by proportion, and the quick chatter climbs back through 1:10 to 1:24. The return is the written order; the dip itself is a measured change in level.
transitions.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −2.4 dB (0:58), −4.7 (0:59), −18.8 (1:00), −23.0 (1:01); boundary at 1:02 (novelty 0.97). The return of the E♭ material at bar 27 of about 40 is in Lamm’s score (Mutopia, limoges.ly); its placement near 1:02 is by proportion only.

transitions.title: A fermata, then slower bars
transitions.how: Near 1:26 the chatter stops for about a second, probably the fermata that the score places in bar 36. Four slower bars follow, marked “Meno mosso, sempre capriccioso”, and they run straight on into the Catacombs. The score marks a poco accelerando in the last of them, bar 40, before the attacca.
transitions.evidence: A frame-by-frame level pass finds near-silence at 1:26.1–1:27.3; level −7.3 dB (1:24), −30.3 (1:26), −8.8 (1:28). The fermata (bar 36), Meno mosso (bars 37–40) and attacca are in Lamm’s score (Mutopia, limoges.ly); the link between score and pause is by proportion and a single measured gap.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
